What belongs in a .gitignore

A .gitignore file tells Git which files to leave out of your repository. Get it right and your history stays clean and safe. Get it wrong and you either commit noise or leak a secret. Here is what to ignore, and what to keep.

The three things worth ignoring

Almost everything you want out of a repository falls into one of three groups.

  • Generated output. Anything a build step produces from your source, like node_modules/, dist/, target/, or __pycache__/. It can be rebuilt, so committing it just bloats the history and causes merge conflicts.
  • Secrets and local config. Files like .env, private keys, and credentials. These should never enter a repository, because once something is committed it stays in the history even after you delete it.
  • Editor and operating system clutter. Files your machine leaves behind, such as .DS_Store on a Mac, Thumbs.db on Windows, or an editor's .idea/ folder. They mean nothing to anyone else on the project.

What to keep, so nobody is stuck

The mistake in the other direction is ignoring too much. Lock files such as package-lock.json or Cargo.lock belong in the repository, because they pin the exact versions everyone should install. An example config, like .env.example with the keys but no values, is worth keeping so a new person knows what settings the project expects. The generator keeps these by using a rule like !.env.example, where the leading ! means "do not ignore this one".

Order and combining stacks

A real project often needs several sets of rules at once. A web app might use Node, plus your operating system, plus your editor. You can stack these safely, since a .gitignore is just a list of patterns read from top to bottom. That is why the gitignore generator lets you pick as many as you need and stitches them into one file with a heading for each.
